source_text: Porro hinc post modicum: Per quid igitur sunt sub diabolo parvuli, qui de corporibus nascuntur quae fecit Deus, de commixtione sexus quem distinxit formando, sed benedicendo coniunxit, et fecunditatem inserendo multiplicavit Deus, et ipsos parvulos de materia seminis fecit Deus? Si per Deum materiam corporum, per Deum genitalia corporum, per Deum commixtionem genitalium, per Deum etiam vim seminum, per Deum quoque omnium nascentium formam atque vitam existere confiteris; quid putas remansisse, propter quod diabolo tot Dei opera transcribas? [n16] Ergo haeresim vocas alterius disputationis corpus, cuius membra omnia recta atque catholica confiteris.
pass_a_gloss: Further from here after a little: Through what therefore are the little ones under the devil, who are born from bodies which God made, from the mingling of the sex which he distinguished by forming, but joined by blessing, and multiplied fertility by inserting it, and the little ones themselves God made from the matter of seed? If you confess that through God the matter of bodies, through God the genital parts of bodies, through God the mingling of the genitals, through God also the force of seeds, through God also the form and life of all who are born exist; what do you think has remained, on account of which you would transfer so many works of God to the devil? Therefore you call heresy the body of another disputation, whose members you confess all to be right and catholic.

lemmas.lexica: LS parvulus; Blaise infants as Julian's test case

pass_b_english: A little later comes this: “Through what, then, are infants under the devil? They are born from bodies God made, from the union of sexes that God distinguished in forming them, joined in blessing them, and multiplied by implanting fertility; and God made the infants themselves from the material of seed. If you acknowledge that the material of bodies, their reproductive organs, the union of those organs, the power of seeds, and the form and life of everyone born all exist through God, what do you think is left for which you can transfer so many of God’s works to the devil?” (Augustine, On Marriage and Concupiscence 2.5.15). So you call someone else’s argument a heresy as a whole, although you acknowledge that every one of its parts is correct and catholic.

choices.why: Julian defends marital union (commixtio) as God's work, not the devil's property.
Augustine's quoted claim that the unbaptized remain under the devil; keep the personal devil, not 'evil'.
rejected: under Satan (name not in the Latin here)

choices.why: Speechless newborns without rational choice; Julian's test case against inherited sin.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
